sections.html:
• Name: Tangerine-head Crab
  • Other names: Orange Vampire Crab, Red Tomato Crab, Indonesian Freshwater Crab
  • Scientific name: Geosesarma krathing
  • Type: semi-terrestrial crab
  • Minimum tank size: 5 gallons (~20 litres)
  • Breeding: easy to medium
  • Carapace size: 1–1.5 cm
  • Leg span: 3–4 cm
  • Aquarium type: paludarium (a tank with both terrestrial and aquatic freshwater elements)
  • Humidity: 75% and higher
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: omnivorous
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Colour: orange with yellow eyes

Tangerine-head crabs (Geosesarma krathing) originate from eastern Thailand in Chanthaburi Province, near the Cambodian border. The species is named after the area where it was collected, Krathing. They were described in 1992 and appeared in the pet trade in 2007.

These little crabs live in forests at and near the bank of the province's main river. They are often called tree-climbing crabs because they climb bushes and trees along the riverbank. They do not depend on saltwater for development at any stage of their life.

The minimum recommended tank size is 5 gallons (20 litres). The bigger the tank, the better for setting up a paludarium with diverse areas to dwell in. These crabs are great escape artists, so a tight-fitting lid is essential.

The land area should take 90% of the space or more. Adult crabs spend most of their time on land; only baby crabs use water.

These crabs are hardy by nature and highly suitable for paludariums. Instead of a complex tank setup, you can use a big water bowl, large enough to completely submerge the crabs. They cannot stay in water for long and will drown, so provide a variety of surfaces to get out of the water. Water bowls make water changes very easy and no filter is needed to keep it clean.

They need only freshwater. If you use tap water, add Seachem Prime to remove chlorine and chloramine. This water conditioner also binds heavy metals, ammonia, nitrites and nitrates for up to 48 hours.

Humidity: they are fairly resilient to humidity fluctuations, but around 75% or higher is recommended. Unstable humidity is one reason people fail to keep them.

Substrate: peat, earth, sand or a sand-earth mixture to nibble at and excavate in. The land part should reflect a rainforest; coconut fibre works best. Keep it moist enough that it holds its shape when squeezed. Add leaves, pieces of bark and some plants.

Lighting: no special requirements; adapt it to the plants in the paludarium.

Decorations and plants: they appreciate leaves, rocks, wood, plants, PVC pipes and so on. They do not eat healthy plants and benefit from live plants by collecting bacteria and microorganisms off them. They are terrestrial in habits and do not require water acclimation.
Acceptable temperatures range from 18 to 30°C, with around 22–24°C being optimal. Humidity around 75% or higher. Nitrate below 20 ppm.

• Filter: sponge filters
  • Air pump: Tetra Whisper
  • Heater: Zoo Med Repti Therm Under Tank Heater
  • Humidity and temperature: AcuRite 00613 Indoor Thermometer & Hygrometer
  • Inert substrate: Zoo Med Hermit Crab Sand, Carib Sea sand, etc.
  • Decor: Malaysian driftwood, PVC pipes, coconuts, crab climbing wall

Tangerine-head crabs are predominantly omnivorous. In a study, biologists found in their stomachs 77% soil/substrate, 13% wood chips, 6% leaves, 3% roots and 1% insect and flower pieces. They prefer detritus and plant parts but are not complete vegetarians, and the diet can change with the season.

Give them organic food such as bloodworms, detritus worms or mussels once or twice a week.

  • Shrimp pellets
  • Shrimp granules
  • Fish food (TetraMin flakes, etc.)
  • Shrimp food (Hikari Shrimp Cuisine, algae wafers, brine shrimp, etc.)
  • Frozen bloodworms
  • Vegetables such as spinach, peas, squash, leafy greens

Give different types of food to supply all necessary microelements. Add Indian almond leaves, dead beech or oak leaves regularly, as they feed on these and need the detritus from the leaves.

Tangerine-head crabs are shy and nocturnal, but from time to time they are seen at dusk or even during the day. They are active and social, and not territorial like most crabs. There are no fights for territory and dominance; they enjoy the company of their own kind. Larger colonies often have more active members that venture out more often.

They do not like intruders of other crab species and can fight with them. When threatened or startled they escape or take cover; they are entirely defenceless.

Although they often dig into the substrate, they are not a burrowing genus. Instead of sitting in dens, they prefer to climb everywhere and are active on the surface.

Like all crustaceans they molt to grow. After molting, a crab may look dead but isn't; it hides until the new shell hardens. Molting is the most vulnerable time, so provide many hiding places or other crabs may eat a molted one. Do not throw away old exoskeletons: they contain lots of minerals and the crabs will eat them after some time.

Tank mates: they do well in a community of their own kind. Keeping other Geosesarma (Red Devil crabs, Vampire crabs) or Metasesarma (Marble crabs, Red Apple crabs) leads to conflicts. If the paludarium is large enough, dwarf shrimp and fish can be kept with them. They are generally non-aggressive and many aquarists keep them safely with adult shrimp and snails, but crabs may catch baby shrimp now and then. Bad tank mates: larger or aggressive fish, any crayfish, other crab species.

Tangerine-head crabs are sexually dimorphic, although sexing is difficult because of their small size.

  • Abdomen: males have a narrow, slimmer plate while females have a broad plate on the belly.
  • Claws: males have larger and sometimes brighter claws; females' claws are about half that size.

Size is not a reliable way to sex them: males and females are the same size, and fully grown females can be a few millimetres bigger.

If a female is interested in mating, she allows a male to approach and flip her upside down, and the male wraps himself around her to fertilise. Size at maturity is about 8–10 mm.

In nature the breeding season is from January to April. After mating, females keep the fertilised eggs under the tail until they hatch 2 months later. Before hatching, females become more secretive and hide almost all the time. The average clutch is 50 eggs, and fecundity increases with body size.

Development is direct (no larval stages): females give birth to live, fully formed miniatures of the adults. Freshly hatched young are very small and cannot live separately from the mother. They stay with her for several weeks until they become independent; then it is advisable to separate the adults from the young in a rearing container to reduce cannibalism. Otherwise only a few young reach adulthood.

Unlike adults, young crabs spend most of their time in or near the water, becoming more terrestrial as they mature. Young crabs can also become prey for siblings during molting, so provide as many hiding places as possible and ideally separate them by size.

Fully grown they are small: shell width about 1–1.5 cm, up to 3–4 cm across the leg span. They are named for the bright orange to red colour of the carapace and claws. Their claws do not open very wide and are better suited to picking up detritus or moving soft soil. Life span in an aquarium is usually 1.5–2 years under optimal conditions. They are excellent scavengers, become less shy over time and suit a nano paludarium.
